name: RISC-V RV64 ABI

stack.notes: Stack grows downward. 16-byte alignment required at public interfaces (function call boundaries). No red zone because asynchronous events (interrupts, exceptions) can occur at any time on bare-metal and must use a reliable stack pointer.

callingConvention.name: RISC-V ELF psABI

variadicRules.notes: Variadic functions conservatively spill all 8 integer argument registers (a0-a7) to the stack in the register save area. The va_list is a simple struct containing a pointer to the stack overflow area. Unlike x86_64 SysV, RISC-V does not track which registers have been consumed — it always spills every argument register.

aggregatePassing.rule: Structs ≤ 2×XLEN bytes (≤ 16 bytes on RV64) are passed in integer registers (if contain ints/pointers) or FP registers (if contain only floats/doubles)
aggregatePassing.memoryThreshold: Structs > 2×XLEN bytes (16 bytes) or containing unaligned fields are passed on the stack

simdRules.notes: With the V extension, vector registers (v0-v31) are used for SIMD arguments following the RVV calling convention. Vector arguments are passed in v8-v23 for non-tail-call, callee-saved v8-v9.

callingConvention.hvaRules: Homogeneous vector aggregates are passed in consecutive vector registers (v8-v23) under the RVV extension

stackFrame.notes: RISC-V uses a convention-based frame pointer (s0/fp) rather than a hardware requirement. Leaf functions that do not modify the stack may omit frame pointer setup entirely. When used, the frame pointer points to the saved s0 value on the stack.

simple.title: Simple integer addition
simple.llvmIR:
define i64 @add(i64 %a, i64 %b) #0 {
entry:
  %a.addr = alloca i64, align 8
  %b.addr = alloca i64, align 8
  store i64 %a, ptr %a.addr, align 8
  store i64 %b, ptr %b.addr, align 8
  %0 = load i64, ptr %a.addr, align 8
  %1 = load i64, ptr %b.addr, align 8
  %add = add nsw i64 %0, %1
  ret i64 %add
}
simple.notes: a in a0 (x10), b in a1 (x11). Return in a0. Single-instruction addition — the canonical RISC two-address operation. No stack frame needed for leaf functions.

complex.title: Struct passing (aggregate in registers and stack)
complex.llvmIR:
define i64 @compute(i64 %p.coerce0, i64 %p.coerce1, i64 %extra) #0 {
entry:
  %p.coerce0.addr = alloca i64, align 8
  %p.coerce1.addr = alloca i64, align 8
  %extra.addr = alloca i64, align 8
  store i64 %p.coerce0, ptr %p.coerce0.addr, align 8
  store i64 %p.coerce1, ptr %p.coerce1.addr, align 8
  store i64 %extra, ptr %extra.addr, align 8
  %0 = load i64, ptr %p.coerce0.addr, align 8
  %1 = load i64, ptr %p.coerce1.addr, align 8
  %mul = mul nsw i64 %0, %1
  %2 = load i64, ptr %extra.addr, align 8
  %add = add nsw i64 %mul, %2
  ret i64 %add
}
complex.assembly:
mul     a0, a0, a1
add     a0, a0, a2
ret
complex.notes: Point is 16 bytes (2×XLEN), fits in two integer registers: p.x in a0, p.y in a1. extra in a2. The struct is flattened into registers — no memory indirection needed. Structs > 16 bytes would be passed on the stack.

variadic.title: Variadic function (printf-like)
variadic.assembly:
sum_ints:
        addi    sp, sp, -160
        sd      ra, 152(sp)
        sd      s0, 144(sp)
        sd      s1, 136(sp)
        sd      a0, 112(sp)
        sd      a1, 120(sp)
        sd      a2, 128(sp)
        sd      a3, 136(sp)
        sd      a4, 144(sp)
        sd      a5, 152(sp)
        sd      a6, 160(sp)
        sd      a7, 168(sp)
        addi    s0, sp, 160
        mv      s1, zero
        # ... loop loading from saved area ...
        ld      ra, 152(sp)
        ld      s0, 144(sp)
        ld      s1, 136(sp)
        addi    sp, sp, 160
        ret
variadic.notes: Variadic functions conservatively spill ALL 8 integer argument registers (a0-a7) to a register save area on the stack. The va_list struct { void *__stack } points to the overflow area past the saved registers. Unlike x86_64 SysV, there is no gp_offset/fp_offset tracking — every register is always spilled.

gccImplementation.notes: GCC implements the RISC-V psABI in riscv.cc. It defines RISCV_CC_RISCV as the C calling convention and handles variadic calls by saving all argument registers to the stack unconditionally. Frame layout uses a variable-size frame with optional frame pointer.

why.question: Why does RISC-V have a hardwired zero register (x0)?
why.answer: The zero register eliminates many instructions that other ISAs need. Loading a constant zero is free (mv rd, x0). Comparisons against zero, unconditional jumps, and many other patterns become single instructions without needing an explicit constant load. This was a deliberate RISC design choice that simplified the hardware — the register file physically ties x0 to zero — and reduced code size for common idioms.

why.question: Why does RISC-V have no red zone?
why.answer: RISC-V targets bare-metal and embedded systems where asynchronous interrupts and exceptions can occur at any instruction boundary. An interrupt handler must be able to use the stack immediately without first checking whether the interrupted function is in a red zone. Unlike x86_64 SysV where the OS guarantees no interrupts will touch the red zone (by setting up a separate interrupt stack), RISC-V makes no such guarantee — it keeps the ABI simple and portable across all environments from RTOS to Linux.

why.question: Why does RISC-V use 8 integer argument registers instead of 6?
why.answer: RISC-V was designed from the start with 8 argument registers (a0-a7) to reduce stack traffic. The 8-register design was motivated by profiling showing that most functions have 8 or fewer arguments. Having 8 registers eliminates stack operations for the vast majority of function calls, improving performance on the simple, in-order cores that are RISC-V's primary targets. This is the same philosophy as AArch64 (which also has 8 integer argument registers) and is more generous than x86_64 SysV (6 registers).

why.question: Why does the variadic calling convention spill all argument registers unconditionally?
why.answer: Simplicity and correctness at the cost of a few stores. The RISC-V psABI defines va_list as a simple struct { void *__stack } — it contains no gp_offset or fp_offset fields like the x86_64 SysV va_list. Because variadic arguments may be any type and any count, and because the compiler cannot know at the ABI level which register types a particular argument uses, all 8 integer registers are always saved. This avoids complex tracking logic in the hardware and keeps the ABI specification minimal. The cost of 8 extra stores is negligible compared to the function call overhead.

why.question: Why is the return address stored in a register (ra) instead of pushed to the stack?
why.answer: JAL and JALR instructions store the return address directly in the ra register (x1) rather than pushing it onto the stack. This eliminates a memory store on every function call. Only functions that themselves call other functions need to save ra to the stack (since a nested call will overwrite it). Leaf functions — which are extremely common — avoid the stack entirely. This is a classic RISC optimization that trades register pressure for reduced memory traffic.

why.question: Why does RISC-V use a convention-based frame pointer instead of requiring one?
why.answer: RISC-V does not mandate a frame pointer — s0/fp is used by convention, not hardware requirement. Leaf functions and functions with small fixed-size frames can omit frame pointer setup entirely, freeing s0 as a general-purpose callee-saved register. This is important because RISC-V has only 12 callee-saved integer registers (s0-s11), and every one counts for register allocation. The optional frame pointer also simplifies simple debuggers and profilers — when present, the frame pointer chain provides a reliable stack walk; when absent, DWARF unwind info serves the same purpose.
